claims.text: The target alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
Optimizing valence electron concentration will enhance superconductivity in the target high-entropy alloy.
The superconductivity enhancement from VEC optimization occurs through changes in electron-phonon coupling.
Changing the relative proportions of constituent elements can be used to vary VEC.
VEC can be varied systematically while preserving a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Controlled arc melting and consistent heat treatment under inert, Ti-gettered Ar will ensure sample homogeneity.
The BCC lattice and local atomic arrangement control the alloy's electronic states.
The BCC lattice and local atomic arrangement modulate electron-phonon interactions.
Variations in VEC shift the density of states at the Fermi level.
Shifts in the density of states at the Fermi level modify electron-phonon coupling strength.
An optimal VEC produces more favorable superconducting pairing conditions.
Departures from the optimal VEC reduce Tc or the superconducting volume fraction.
VEC-optimized alloys will have a significantly higher Tc than the baseline alloy.
VEC-optimized alloys will exhibit sharper resistive transitions and larger superconducting fractions than the baseline.
The baseline composition is not optimized for superconductivity and is similar to previously reported Nb-Ta-dominated or titanium-rich systems.
The proposed VEC relationship is applicable only to stable, minimally inhomogeneous, single-phase BCC alloys with minimal secondary phases and ordering.
Chemical inhomogeneity, ordering, or secondary-phase formation may obscure the effect of VEC on superconductivity.
Failure of optimized-VEC samples to improve Tc or superconducting fraction, or absence of a systematic VEC correlation, would falsify the hypothesis.
